title: Pointers and Memory
tagline: Addresses, dereferencing, lifetime and allocators, one byte at a time
description: A whole course on the thing that makes C and C++ hard: memory. What an address is, reading and writing through pointers, pointer arithmetic and strides, reinterpreting bytes, structs and offsets, following chains of pointers, the stack, the heap and object lifetime, ownership, leaks, smart pointers and views, and finally writing your own arena, pool and free-list allocators and seeing how virtual memory and pages work. It assumes the first milestones of the C++ course.

milestones.title: Addresses and Dereferencing
milestones.blurb: Memory as a row of numbered bytes, pointers as variables that hold addresses, reading and writing through them, pointers as parameters, and the null, dangling and wild pointers that crash programs.

lessons.title: Memory Is a Row of Bytes
lessons.summary: A program's memory is one long row of bytes, each with a number called its address. Every variable occupies a few of those bytes, sizeof says how many, and & gives the address of the first one. Addresses are written in hexadecimal and change from run to run.

lessons.title: Pointers Are Variables That Hold Addresses
lessons.summary: A pointer is an ordinary variable whose value is an address. Its type says what kind of value lives at that address. Declaring, initialising and printing pointers, nullptr for "no address", and why int* and double* are different types even though both are 8 bytes.

lessons.title: Dereferencing
lessons.summary: The * operator follows a pointer to the object at its address, to read it or to write it. Two pointers to one object see each other's writes. The -> operator reaches a member through a pointer, and const can protect either the pointer or the value it points at.

lessons.title: Pointers as Parameters
lessons.summary: C++ passes arguments by copying them, so a function cannot change the caller's variables, unless it receives their addresses. Out-parameters, swap, returning several results, optional parameters with nullptr, and when a reference is the better choice.

lessons.title: Null, Dangling and Wild Pointers
lessons.summary: The three kinds of bad pointer - null, dangling and wild - what each one is, what happens when you follow it, why the crash often appears far from the bug, and the habits that keep pointers valid.

tasks.title: Handles that know when they dangle

milestones.title: Pointer Arithmetic and Arrays
milestones.blurb: Arrays as consecutive memory, how pointer arithmetic scales by the type, walking buffers with begin and end pointers, 2D data and strides, and looking at the raw bytes behind any value.

lessons.title: Arrays Are Consecutive Memory
lessons.summary: An array is its elements placed one after another with no gaps, so element i sits at the start address plus i times the element size. An array's name turns into a pointer to its first element when passed to a function, which is why the function loses the length and sizeof stops working.

lessons.title: Pointer Arithmetic
lessons.summary: Adding n to a pointer moves it n elements, not n bytes, because the compiler multiplies by the size of the type. Subtracting two pointers counts the elements between them. Comparing pointers, the one-past-the-end pointer, and the rules that keep arithmetic inside an array.

lessons.title: Walking Buffers
lessons.summary: Loops that move a pointer instead of an index, begin and end pointers as in the standard library, C strings as pointers to a run of chars ending in zero, and the classic string functions written by hand.

lessons.title: Rows, Columns and Strides
lessons.summary: Two-dimensional data is stored as one long row of memory, row after row. The index of (x, y) is y times the row length plus x, and the row length in memory, the stride, can be longer than the visible width. Sub-images that share memory, and why walking along rows is faster than down columns.

lessons.title: Looking at Raw Bytes
lessons.summary: Any object's bytes can be read through an unsigned char pointer. Reading them as a different type is a different matter - the strict aliasing rule forbids most pointer casts, so memcpy and std::bit_cast are the correct tools. Byte order, swapping it, and the casts C++ offers.

milestones.title: Structures and Pointer Chains
milestones.blurb: Where each member of a struct sits, pointers to pointers, following a chain of pointers from a base address through offsets, linked structures, and pointers to functions.

lessons.title: Structs in Memory
lessons.summary: A struct's members sit at fixed offsets from its start, in the order they are declared, with padding added so each member is suitably aligned. offsetof gives a member's offset, the arrow operator is "base address plus offset", and reordering members can make a struct smaller.

lessons.title: Pointers to Pointers
lessons.summary: A pointer is a variable, so it has an address, and a pointer can point at it. int** lets a function change which address the caller's pointer holds. Arrays of pointers, argv, and the pointer-to-pointer trick that removes items from a linked list without special cases.

lessons.title: Following Pointer Chains
lessons.summary: Real programs reach data through several levels of pointers - a game reaches a player's health through the world, the level and the player. A chain can be written as a base address and a list of offsets, followed one read at a time with a null check at every step. Why chains survive restarts when single addresses do not.

lessons.title: Linked Structures
lessons.summary: Data structures held together by pointers - singly and doubly linked lists, a sentinel node that removes the special cases, trees - what they cost in memory and speed compared with an array, and the intrusive lists that games and operating systems use.

tasks.title: A doubly linked list with a sentinel

lessons.title: Function Pointers and Callbacks
lessons.summary: Functions live in memory too, and a function pointer holds the address of one. The declaration syntax and how to tame it with using, tables of functions, C-style callbacks with a void* context, how virtual functions are tables of function pointers, and std::function.

projects.title: Insert with a pointer to a pointer
Pointer paths in an address space

milestones.title: Lifetime: Stack, Heap and Static
milestones.blurb: Where memory comes from, the stack up close, the heap with new, delete, malloc and free, who owns what, and finding the leaks when nobody does.

lessons.title: Where Memory Comes From
lessons.summary: A running program's address space holds its code, its static data, one stack per thread and the heap. Each object gets one of four lifetimes - static, automatic, dynamic or thread - and the lifetime decides where it lives, when it starts and when its address stops being valid.

tasks.title: Things that live for the whole program

lessons.title: The Stack Up Close
lessons.summary: Each function call pushes a frame holding the return address and the function's locals; returning pops it. The stack pointer moves down as frames are added. Why a pointer to a local dangles after the return, what a stack overflow is, and how writing past a local array can overwrite a return address.

lessons.title: The Heap
lessons.summary: new and delete, new[] and delete[], malloc and free - what each does, why they must be paired exactly, what the allocator keeps next to every block, and the bugs that come from getting a pair wrong - double frees, mismatched frees, and memory that was never initialised.

lessons.title: Ownership
lessons.summary: Every heap object needs exactly one owner responsible for freeing it; every other pointer to it only borrows. Owning versus borrowing pointers, transferring ownership, who frees what across a function or library boundary, and writing ownership down so the next reader does not have to guess.

tasks.title: An inventory that owns its items

lessons.title: Leaks and How to Find Them
lessons.summary: A leak is memory nobody frees. Why leaks matter in programs that run for hours, how the MSVC debug heap reports them at exit with an allocation number you can break on, heap snapshots in Visual Studio, AddressSanitizer for leaks and use-after-free, and counting your own allocations.

projects.title: A debug heap of your own

milestones.title: Managing Memory Safely
milestones.blurb: RAII, unique_ptr and custom deleters, shared_ptr and weak_ptr, views that do not own like span and string_view, and copying and moving a type that owns memory.

lessons.title: RAII
lessons.summary: Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation - tie every resource to an object whose destructor releases it, and C++ frees it on every path out of a scope, early returns and exceptions included. Writing small owning wrappers, scope guards, and why this one idea removes most leaks.

lessons.title: unique_ptr
lessons.summary: std::unique_ptr is a pointer that owns its object and deletes it when it goes away. It cannot be copied, only moved, so ownership is written in the type. make_unique, get, release and reset, unique_ptr in containers and as return values, and custom deleters for FILE*, HANDLE and anything else.

lessons.title: shared_ptr and weak_ptr
lessons.summary: std::shared_ptr shares ownership through a reference count kept in a control block, and deletes the object when the last owner goes. What it costs, the cycles that make it leak, std::weak_ptr for observing without owning, and when shared ownership is really the right answer.

tasks.title: A cache that does not keep things alive

lessons.title: Views That Do Not Own
lessons.summary: std::span and std::string_view are a pointer and a length bundled together - a cheap, safe way to borrow a sequence without copying or owning it. Passing them to functions, slicing them, and the one way they go wrong - outliving what they view.

lessons.title: Copy and Move for Owning Types
lessons.summary: A class that owns memory must decide what copying and moving mean. The rule of five, a deep copy, a move that steals the pointer and leaves the source empty, copy-and-swap for safe assignment, self-assignment, and the rule of zero - letting members that already own do it all.

projects.title: A buffer with the rule of five
A string with a small buffer

milestones.title: Allocators and Virtual Memory
milestones.blurb: How an allocator works inside, arenas and pools of your own, a free list with splitting and joining, virtual memory and pages, and a field guide to memory bugs.

lessons.title: How an Allocator Works
lessons.summary: Inside malloc and new - big regions carved into blocks, headers that record each block's size, free lists, first fit, splitting and joining blocks, alignment, fragmentation, and the size classes that make modern allocators fast.

lessons.title: Arena Allocators
lessons.summary: An arena hands out memory by moving one pointer forward and frees everything at once by moving it back. Bump allocation, alignment, frame arenas reset every frame, markers for rewinding part of an arena, and the rules for what may live in one.

lessons.title: Pool Allocators
lessons.summary: A pool hands out blocks of one fixed size from a single region. Free blocks are linked into a list through their own memory, so allocating and freeing are a couple of pointer moves, with no headers and no fragmentation. Building one, and where games use them.

tasks.title: A pool with a free list inside

lessons.title: Virtual Memory and Pages
lessons.summary: Every address a program uses is virtual. The processor translates it, one 4 KB page at a time, through page tables the operating system maintains. Pages that are reserved, committed or free, page protection, page faults, guard pages, and what an access violation really is.

lessons.title: A Field Guide to Memory Bugs
lessons.summary: Everything in this course turned into a way of working - reading a crash's address, recognising the debug fill patterns, the symptom-to-cause table, data breakpoints, AddressSanitizer and page heap, and the habits that stop the bugs being written in the first place.

tasks.title: What does this address tell you?
